overview: The file consists of a two-page State Department “List of Papers” indexing correspondence and reports, chiefly from 1939, concerning Japanese merchant shipping. The indexed material covers monthly shipping conditions in the Japanese Empire, alleged freight-rate cutting and government discrimination against American carriers, the activities of Yamashita Kisen and Osaka Shosen, prospective international and coastal services, personnel at American President Lines, and the launchings of the Sakura Maru and Kokoku Maru at Nagasaki. Several entries direct researchers to related papers in decimal file 800.8890.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Merchant Vessels—Japan, entries 535–549
subfiles.about: A two-page register summarizes State Department papers concerning Japanese merchant shipping and related American commercial interests.
subfiles.summary: The register lists dispatches and departmental communications dating principally from 1939, with an earlier report on shipping during October 1938. Subjects include shipping conditions, Japanese freight-rate practices, alleged discrimination against American President Lines, proposed international services, consolidation of Japan-China coastal traffic under the Tōa Kaiun Kaisha, and personnel changes at Yokohama. It also records the December 1939 launchings of the Sakura Maru and Kokoku Maru at Nagasaki and supplies cross-references to related 800.8890 files. OCR damage and table misalignment obscure some dates and appear to run portions of entries 544–547 together.

interest: This register is useful chiefly as a finding aid: it maps a dispersed group of consular reports, departmental communications, newspaper clippings, and Maritime Commission material that may otherwise be difficult to locate. Its entries reveal how closely American officials monitored both Japanese state support for shipping and the competitive practices of individual Japanese lines. The juxtaposition of commercial disputes, regional route expansion, coastal consolidation, and new ship construction offers a compact view of Japan’s maritime expansion immediately before the Pacific War; the Nagasaki entries also preserve precise launching dates and shipyard information.
